passage:
"You don't have to talk," Manoj said, dropping his bag on Dhruv's bed.
"I don't know what to say."
"Cool. I brought the chess set. Or we just sit."
They sat. The fan clicked. Ten minutes went by.
"Everybody keeps telling me what to do," Dhruv said at last. "Be strong. Keep busy. Eat something."
"I'm not telling you anything."
"I know. That's why it helps." Dhruv rubbed his eyes. "Today I want company but no talking. Tomorrow I might want to talk about Aaji."
"Text me which one. I'll come either way."
"Maybe chess, actually. Badly."
Manoj set out the pieces. "I'll play worse."

qa.q: What did Manoj bring with him?
Why did Dhruv say Manoj's silence helps?
qa.a: Everybody else keeps telling Dhruv what to do, so Manoj not giving advice feels like relief.

qa.q: How can Dhruv get the help he needs in the coming days?
qa.a: He can tell Manoj which one he wants that day: company, space, a distraction or a chance to talk about Aaji.

qa.q: What might it be like for Manoj to sit without giving advice?
qa.a: It may feel awkward not to fix anything, yet Manoj chooses to stay and brings chess so there are options.

grounding: A friend sits with a grieving teen without advice and it helps; the teen says what he needs, whether company, quiet or distraction.

passage:
Dear Anand,
I never said thank you properly for the evening after Appa's funeral, so here it is.
Everyone else came with advice. Be strong for your mother. He's in a better place. Time heals. I know they meant well, but every sentence made me feel more alone.
You just sat next to me on the stairs outside our flat for two hours. You didn't say anything clever. You passed me your water bottle and your handkerchief, and once you said, 'I'm here.' That was it. It was the only time that week I could actually breathe.
I've been thinking about what helps, so I can tell you. Some days I'll want you to talk about anything but Appa: cricket, exams, your terrible jokes. Some days I'll want to talk about him. And some days I'll need to be alone, and it won't be about you.
Is that okay? I'll try to tell you which day it is.
Yamini

qa.q: Where did Anand sit with Yamini after the funeral?
qa.a: On the stairs outside the flat, for two hours.

qa.q: How did the advice from others make Yamini feel?
qa.a: Yamini felt more alone with every well-meant sentence, even though people meant well.

qa.q: Why is it helpful that Yamini names different kinds of days?
qa.a: It lets Anand know when to distract, when to listen and when to give space, without guessing.

qa.q: What was it like for Anand to sit there without speaking?
qa.a: Anand may have felt unsure what to say, but staying close with water and a handkerchief showed quiet care 🤍

grounding: A letter from a grieving teen thanking a friend who simply sat with them, and naming whether they need space, company or distraction.

passage: People ask what helped most after Nani died. I'm Vaibhav, and my answer surprises them: my friend Afreen doing nothing. Nani raised me, so when she went, I stopped talking at school. Everyone had advice: go for a walk, keep busy, pray. Afreen just started sitting next to me at lunch. No questions. She'd eat her paratha and I'd stare at mine. Some days she'd hum. It was the only time the knot in my stomach loosened. After a week I found words. I told her, 'Some days I want you to talk about anything else. Some days I want to talk about Nani. Some days I just want to be alone.' She said, 'Tell me which, and that's what I'll do.' And she did. So if you ask me, the best thing you can do for a grieving friend is sit down, and let them tell you the rest.

qa.q: What did Afreen do at lunch after Nani died?
qa.a: She started sitting next to Vaibhav at lunch, eating her paratha; some days she'd hum. No questions.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling while sitting with Afreen?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt the knot in the stomach loosen, a small relief from the heavy grief.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do once the words came?
qa.a: Vaibhav told Afreen what was needed on different days: distraction, talking about Nani, or being alone.

qa.q: How does Afreen respond to that request?
qa.a: She accepts it simply, promising to do whichever Vaibhav asks, and keeps her word.

grounding: A spoken account of a grieving teen helped by a friend who sat without advice, then naming whether they needed space, company or distraction.
